analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates up to 5 points for firms whose top pay is over 50 times median worker pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in November 2019 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a tax surcharge on large corporations — those with average gross receipts of $100 million or more — based on the gap between their highest-paid employee and their median worker. A firm paying its top employee 50 to 100 times the median would pay a 0.5 percentage point higher corporate rate; a ratio above 500 to 1 would add 5 points to the 21% corporate rate. The idea is to give corporations a financial reason to either raise typical worker pay or rein in executive compensation, and to raise some revenue either way.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations with extreme pay gaps, who gain if firms respond by lifting median pay or narrowing top pay; and the general public, which receives revenue from the surcharge.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at big firms with wide pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Corporations whose highest-paid employee earns more than 50 times the median worker's pay face a corporate rate increase of 0.5 percentage points, rising in steps to 5 points at ratios above 500 to 1, on top of the 21% corporate rate.
The measurement covers the highest-compensated employee whether or not that person is the CEO, so the penalty reaches any extreme pay gap at the top of the company.

The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio — for example, by replacing low-paid employees with outside contractors — and exempts private corporations with average gross receipts under $100 million.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with extreme executive pay ratios and, through them, their shareholders; executives face pressure on their own compensation, and companies bear the cost of measuring and reporting pay ratios.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is modest — 0.5 to 5 percentage points — so a firm with a 300-to-1 pay gap could absorb the extra tax rather than change its pay structure, raising little money and changing little behavior.

The bill builds on the SEC's existing pay-ratio disclosure rules, so compliance is an added reporting cost for covered corporations, and Treasury must write new anti-avoidance rules because companies can otherwise manipulate the ratio through contractors or workforce composition.
A company could avoid the tax by raising only median pay, by cutting jobs at the bottom, or by restructuring, none of which necessarily improves conditions for the workers the bill aims to help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is real but gentle: rather than capping pay or mandating raises, it uses a graduated tax penalty to make extreme pay gaps more expensive, while exempting small private firms. Its main cost is compliance and tax planning at large corporations; its main weakness is that the penalty may be small enough to be absorbed without changing behavior. As a first-of-its-kind lever on executive-to-worker pay inequality, it is modest in scale on both sides.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on November 13, 2019, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Finance.
The bill had one cosponsor, Senator Elizabeth Warren, who joined Sanders in introducing it.
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off: their 21% flat corporate rate was never touched, and no pay-ratio tax ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big corporations kept the flat 21% rate

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on November 13, 2019.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Senate cosponsor.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Senator Sanders' behalf when it was formally presented to the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, took no action on it; it received no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; support in the Senate was two senators (an Independent sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor), and no Republican backed the bill.

industries.industry: Large public and private corporations (gross receipts of $100 million or more)
industries.note: The bill would add up to 5 percentage points to their 21% corporate rate in proportion to their pay gap, and would require pay-ratio reporting and anti-avoidance compliance. Firms with extreme ratios would face a choice between the tax, raising median pay, or cutting top pay. The bill never advanced, so no change occurred.

industries.industry: Executives and top earners at large corporations
industries.note: The surcharge pressures companies to trim or restrain top compensation; a highest-paid employee who is not the CEO would still be counted. Non-CEO top earners are captured by the same measure.

industries.industry: Pay-ratio measurement, accounting, and tax compliance services
industries.note: Calculating and reporting the pay ratio for covered non-SEC filers and under new Treasury rules would create compliance work. The bill never advanced, so this market never materialized.
